# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Gets Upstairs

Turn on a faucet on the fortieth floor of a high-rise and water comes out under pressure, as if by magic. It isn't magic—it's a carefully engineered system of elevation, pumps, tanks, and valves, all working together against the relentless pull of gravity. To understand how it works, let's follow water from a reservoir to a hypothetical apartment building, which we'll call the Meridian Tower, a 40-story building in a mid-sized city.

## The Fundamental Physics: Elevation as Energy

The core insight of water system design is that elevation is stored energy. Water at a high elevation possesses potential energy, and if you give it a path, it will flow downhill, converting that energy into pressure and motion. Every vertical foot of elevation corresponds to roughly 0.433 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure. Engineers call this "head," and it's the currency of water distribution.
